content: Cutaneous infections caused by Mycobacterium marinum have been documented in individuals who own or clean fish tanks. Ectoparasites and endoparasites present significant risks when humans interact with exhibit animals. Sarcoptes scabiei, a skin mite, can infest both humans and animals, including swine, dogs, cats, foxes, cattle, and coyotes. While human infestations from animal sources are typically self-limiting, they can cause skin irritation and itching that may persist for several days and be challenging to diagnose. Avian mite bites have been reported in association with pet gerbils in school environments. Flea bites from animals can increase the risk of infections or allergic reactions, and fleas may also carry tapeworm species that can infect children who accidentally ingest them. Humans can also acquire parasitic infections by ingesting materials contaminated with animal feces or coming into contact with contaminated soil. Effective parasite control through veterinary care, proper animal husbandry, and hand hygiene can significantly reduce the risks associated with ectoparasites and endoparasites. Tuberculosis is another disease of concern in certain animal settings. For instance, in 1996, 12 circus elephant handlers in Illinois were infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis after three elephants died of tuberculosis. Medical evaluations suggested that the elephants were the likely source of exposure for most of the human infections. Similarly, between 1989 and 1991, seven animal handlers at a Louisiana zoo tested positive for tuberculosis following a Mycobacterium bovis outbreak in rhinoceroses and monkeys. Other cases of mycobacterial transmission from animals to animal care staff, without known public transmission, have also been documented. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has established guidelines for removing tuberculosis-infected animals from public settings to mitigate the risk of public exposure. Zoonotic pathogens can also be transmitted through direct or indirect contact with reproductive fluids, aborted fetuses, or newborns from infected animals. This is particularly relevant in agricultural fairs where animals such as cattle, pigs, goats, and sheep are often present. Although the public typically does not have direct contact with animals during birthing, newborns and their mothers may be available for petting afterward. Serious zoonoses, such as Q fever (caused by Coxiella burnetii), leptospirosis, listeriosis, brucellosis, and chlamydiosis, can be acquired through contact with reproductive materials. Coxiella burnetii, a rickettsial organism, primarily infects cattle, sheep, and goats. While it can cause abortion in animals, the infection is often asymptomatic. During birthing, infected animals shed large quantities of organisms, which can become aerosolized. Most individuals exposed to C. burnetii develop asymptomatic infections, but clinical illness can range from acute flu-like symptoms to life-threatening endocarditis. A Q fever outbreak involving 95 confirmed cases and 41 hospitalizations was linked to goats and sheep giving birth at petting zoos in indoor shopping malls. Indoor birthing exhibits may pose an increased risk for Q fever transmission due to inadequate ventilation. Chlamydophila psittaci infections, which cause respiratory disease, are typically acquired from psittacine birds. For example, an outbreak of C. psittaci pneumonia occurred among staff members at the Copenhagen Zoological Garden. Rarely, chlamydial infections acquired from sheep, goats, or birds can result in reproductive complications in women. Influenza virus transmission between humans and animals also has implications for animals in public settings. Sporadic cases and clusters of human infections with swine influenza viruses have been reported since the 1970s, with several cases linked to swine at agricultural fairs. Conversely, human influenza viruses have also been transmitted to swine, as seen during the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, which involved sporadic human-to-swine transmission. Guidelines from multiple organizations have informed recommendations to mitigate the risks of zoonotic disease transmission in public settings. For example, in 2005, North Carolina enacted legislation requiring individuals displaying animals for public contact at agricultural fairs to obtain a permit from the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. Federal agencies and associations in the United States have developed standards and guidelines to reduce risks associated with public contact with animals in zoological parks. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums has accreditation standards to minimize public-animal contact risks. Under the Animal Welfare Act, the USDA licenses and inspects certain animal exhibits, focusing on humane treatment while also addressing animal health and public safety. In 2001, the CDC issued guidelines to reduce the risk of infection with enteric pathogens associated with farm visits. The CDC has also provided recommendations for preventing Salmonella transmission from reptiles, amphibians, and live poultry to humans. The Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology (APIC) and the Animal-Assisted Interventions Working Group (AAI) have developed guidelines to address risks associated with using animals in healthcare settings. The National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians (NASPHV) has compiled measures to reduce human exposure to C. psittaci and rabies virus. Studies in some localities suggest that implementing these recommendations could be improved. Stakeholders should work to ensure comprehensive implementation of these recommendations. Enhanced communication and cooperation among human and animal health agencies, including veterinarians and cooperative extension offices, are essential for addressing zoonotic disease risks effectively.
